highlights.text: core idea of loosing/setting free
a woman ṭuliqat/ṭaluqat is a ṭāliq (plural ṭawāliq)
انطلق = to set off (on an errand)
Shāhid from al-Nābigha, of venom that alternately "lets go" and returns.
one root meaning: sticking fast and staying in place (al-luzūm wa-l-iqāma)
Al-Khalīl defines al-banān as the tips of the fingers of the hands.
as in the verse "no tribe has a banāna above them"
Al-Zajjāj says it means the fingers and all the other limbs, and gives banāna as the singular.
derives four distinct base senses from the root
Al-Khalīl: "abramtu al-amr" = I made the matter firm, settled it.
cited from ʿAlqama's verse on a gazelle-eyed woman's streaked tears
from two base ideas: (1) returning to a thing, and (2) the equality or matching of two things
Hence tabawwaʾū (they settled) and bawwaʾahum Allāh manzila ṣidq (God settled them in a place of truth)
bāʾa bi-dhanbihi = he "returned bearing his sin," as though he went back to his abode carrying it
Ṭarafa ("goodly of dwelling…")
Ibn Fāris derives ب-و-ر from two distinct roots.
On al-Khalīl's authority, البَوَار (bawār) is perishing.
He notes that بُور serves for singular and plural, feminine and masculine alike, citing Q 48:12, "and you were a doomed people."
shown by ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zibaʿrā's line, "my tongue is mending what I tore open when I was worthless."
Ibn al-Aʿrābī: dasā is said of someone who has hidden himself.
a verse that Ibn al-Aʿrābī recited from a man of Ṭayyiʾ: "You are the one who dassayta ʿAmr, so that their women became widows of them, forsaken"
The article gives the meaning as: he has failed who dassā'd his own soul, that is, made it obscure and debased its share.
The core idea is splitting, cleaving, and parting apart, from which the other senses branch.
highlights.note: Editor's statement of the root sense

highlights.text: The word فِئة (party/company of people) is said to derive from this root — a "party" being a portion split off from the whole.
Shāhid from al-Namir b. Tawlab: an ungrazed fāʾw of land, its meadow concealed, "encircled by landmarks."
highlights.note: al-Namir b. Tawlab, lived into Islam

highlights.text: Here fiʾa means both the company of people in general and, specifically, the reserve detachment stationed behind an army, to which fighters fall back if they meet fear or defeat.
Ibn Fāris treats h-l-l as a single sound root meaning "raising the voice".
The hilāl is so called because people raise their voices on seeing it, proclaiming God's greatness and calling out in prayer.
Ibn Aḥmar speaks of riders who "raise their voices at al-Farqad, as the mounted muʿtamir raises his."
from his line "I halhaltu, seeking vengeance for Jābir or Ṣinbil", where the word means he shouted as he pressed on to overtake his quarry
Man / human being (مَرْء).
The feminine is مَرْأَة, regularly lightened to مَرَة
طَعامٌ مَرِئٌ is "wholesome, agreeable food" of good consequence
A verse of Abū Khirāsh (praising a man's gathered virtues — forbearance, kindness, noble lineage) is transmitted by al-Sukkarī with a kasra (al-mirʾ), said to be the dialect of Hudhayl.
"an opening made in something" — piercing, perforating, breaching.
naqaba al-ḥāʾiṭ — to breach/pierce a wall (naqb = a breach or hole).
al-naqīb — the appointed representative of a group: their witness and their guarantor.
naqqabū fī l-bilād, "they traveled through the land," derives from traveling along these mountain-passes (al-nuqūb).
A verse calls such a man a niqāb who "reports the unseen," i.e., uncovers what others can't see.
Ibn Fāris treats q-ṭ-ʿ as a single sound root meaning severing and separating one thing from another.
قَطَعَ / قَطْع — to cut something.
الْقِطْع (kasra) is a portion of the night.
highlights.note: qiṭʿ, a part of the night

highlights.text: الْقَطِيع (one sense): a whip — cited from al-Aʿshā.
he reports an exegesis reading it as self-strangulation (al-ikhtināq), and judges the analogy to the root sound.
A sound triliteral root meaning to wrench or tear a thing loose from a thing.
aqlaʿa ʿan al-amr = he held back from a matter.
aqlaʿat ʿanhu al-ḥummā, "the fever released him"
Cited proverb: "My fat is in my bag" (i.e., my resource is close at hand, within my own keeping).
"Neither a daybūb nor a qalāʿ enters the Garden."
three distinct underlying senses
Qarḥ is a sore or wound on the skin, or the sores (qurūḥ) that break out on the body and hurt.
Cited: Qur'an 3:140, "If a wound touches you, a similar wound has already touched the [other] people" — used of both sides suffering harm in battle.
illustrated with a line from the poet Dhū al-Rumma describing a dark-green meadow with a white patch
one sound root whose core meaning is the opposite of remoteness — nearness.
قَرُبَ / يَقْرُبُ / قُرْبًا, "to be or become near."
قَرِيب means "relative"; qurba and qurbā both mean kinship.
"I have not gone near this matter, nor do I" means one has not touched or become entangled in it.
The core idea is returning / coming back.
The noun مثابة (mathāba) is a place people keep coming back to: "the House is a mathāba for the people."
أثاب / ثوّب — to requite, reward: "God requited him." Zamakhsharī cites the Qurʾān, "have the disbelievers been requited" (83:36)
"draw your garments out of mine" = withdraw and part from me (shāhid from Imruʾ al-Qays, where the garments "slip loose")
linked by the idea of flowing, dropping, and by-products
highlights.note: Editor's summary of the root's shared idea

highlights.text: any open cleft between mountains, hills, and mounds; named from "flowing," because water runs through it.
The compensation due for a slain person: وَدَيْتُه ("I paid his blood-money").
A verse of al-Aʿshā uses a masculine verb (أَوْدَى for أَوْدَتْ) because "the vicissitudes of time" (al-ḥadathān) are intended.
Ibn Sīda holds this is not literal valleys but a metaphor for the poets' shifting speech — like the idiom "I am for you in one valley and you in another."
a single, consistent root whose core meaning is the separation or removal of a thing from what had enveloped it or from what it had been invested with
The base sense: khalaʿtu al-thawb, "I took off the garment."
Ibn Fāris quotes a line of poetry comparing a howling wolf in a desolate valley to "the disowned outcast (al-khalīʿ) burdened with dependents."
He cites a ḥadīth condemning women who seek this kind of separation without cause
Basic sense — thickness/coarseness.
الخِنْزِير (al-khinzīr) — the pig, counted among aggressive wild beasts — is well known
The hand is well-known.
"This estate is in so-and-so's hand" means in his ownership.
"bayna yaday" = before / in front of. Used for whatever lies ahead of you.
cited from Labīd, where the north wind's holding the "rein" pictures its control over marshalling the clouds as "possession of the hand."
the sayings "dust stirs up before the rain" and "cursing flares up before the fighting"
al-zawd is laying in provisions.
Al-zād (provisions) means food for a journey or for staying at home alike
tazawwada ("he took provisions for himself")
Cited in verse from Abū Khirāsh, using tuzīdu ("you provision [someone]").
A proverb says "more hospitable than Zād al-rakb," referring to one or to all three of them.
any deed a person carries away with him — good or bad — is metaphorically called zād ("provision").
